toolCalls.name: StructuredOutput

output.brief:
The overrun is mainly a side effect of not renewing the closing contract, not of the hiring freeze. From 1 April, nightly closing at 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook moved to maintenance staff as call-backs. Each call-back is paid at a 3-hour minimum, even though a closing round takes 30–45 minutes. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. 1,962 of 2,295 call-backs carry the CLOSE code, and none are in Summit Hill, which kept its contract. Holdover overtime, the type vacancies would drive, rose only about 5%, and most of that is the July wage increase. Summit Hill has vacancies but almost no rise. The contract saved $96k, and the call-backs cost about $250k more.

Internal Audit checked the fraud allegation against lock logs and found no padding. Eastgate favoritism is plausible, since the same few people sign up and the sheets were discarded, but it is unproven. The link between overtime and injuries is only an association, because hours worked by the injured staff were never checked.

I'm fairly confident in this. Restore contracted closing, or re-tender it, and track call-back spending. Don't cap overtime, discipline the two employees, or discipline the supervisor. Keep the sign-up sheets from now on. Review the Eastgate assignments, and match injury claims to payroll hours. The eleven-position exemption is not justified by this evidence.
